issues.issue: The definition expressly includes "reservations, exceptions, encroachments, easements, rights-of-way, covenants, conditions, restrictions, leases, and other title exceptions ... affecting Real Property", so Section 7.2's flat prohibition on suffering any Lien to exist would be breached by ordinary title exceptions on every parcel. Only clause (k) of "Permitted Liens" rescues some of them, and whether the two can be read together is not answerable from this definition alone.

After enumerating specific instruments the definition adds "any other agreement entered into, now or in the future, by any Borrower and Lender in connection with this Agreement", so the class of Loan Documents is open-ended. Because Section 8.2 makes breach of any "comparable provision contained in any of the other Loan Documents" an Event of Default, the reach of that catch-all determines the reach of the default clause.

"Material Adverse Change" turns on a "material adverse change in the business, prospects, operations, results of operations, assets, liabilities or financial condition" — with "prospects" and "material" left undefined and no baseline or measurement period stated. The term controls the funding condition in Section 3.3(d) and several representations, so its boundary is squarely contestable.

The $50,000,000 ceiling cannot be reconciled with Section 7.16(b), which caps the Senior Leverage Ratio — Obligations over Tangible Net Worth — at nine-tenths of one percent, permitting only about $5.4 million of Obligations against the $600,000,000 Tangible Net Worth required by Section 3.1(n). Drawing anywhere near the Maximum Revolver Amount would breach the covenant on the first testing date.

The parenthetical "(less portions that are not in compliance with the definition thereof)" subtracts from a quantity already limited to Eligible Notes Receivable, which by definition comply. Whether the parenthetical adds a further haircut, or is mere surplusage, is an ambiguity in the definition's own words.

"New Fund" is keyed to entities formed "after the Effective Date", a term this Agreement never defines — the operative date elsewhere is the "Closing Date", and Section 16.1 speaks only of when the Agreement is "deemed effective". The further requirement that the entity be "funded principally using debt securities" and not "capitalized or otherwise funded with assets of such Borrower" supplies no measurement point either.

Any New Fund is carved out of the definition of "Subsidiary", which means the Section 7.13 prohibition on forming or acquiring a Subsidiary without Lender's consent, and the Section 7.12 restriction on Investments, do not reach it. Whether the Borrowers could form and deal with an affiliated lending fund free of those covenants can only be decided by reading this definition with Sections 7.12 and 7.13.

A Note Receivable is a note evidencing a loan "made or purchased by Fund", but clause (a) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition excludes any loan not "originated by Servicer but ... now held by Fund". The two provisions describe different populations, and which one governs a purchased loan for reporting and eligibility purposes is unresolved.

The definition — "the real property securing an Eligible Note Receivable in which Fund has a title-insured first priority lien, or security title to, that has been assigned or pledged to Lender" — is grammatically broken, so it is unclear whether "that has been assigned or pledged" modifies the real property, the lien, or the Note Receivable. What must have been assigned to Lender before property qualifies as Note Receivable Collateral is therefore uncertain.

"Offering Circular" lumps together the Private Offering Memorandum "as amended from time to time", the LLC operating agreement, subscription agreements and unspecified "related agreements and instruments". Because Section 5.3 warrants that "[a]ny Offering Circular" complies with all applicable securities laws, the open-ended composition of the term fixes the scope of that representation.

"Permitted Discretion" is defined as "reasonable (from the perspective of a secured asset-based lender) business judgment" — a standard measured from one party's own vantage point and nowhere further specified. The term governs reserves, eligibility criteria, Additional Documents, consent to modifications and the materiality judgment in Section 8.16, so its content is repeatedly decisive.

Only clause (e) — sales of Notes Receivable — carries the condition that proceeds be paid directly into a Cash Management Account, while clauses (f) and (g) permit sales of Note Receivable Collateral and of Real Estate Owned with no such condition. Whether the cash-management requirement of Section 2.6(a) nonetheless reaches those proceeds is left open by the enumeration.

Clause (c)'s parenthetical is broken — "so long as such Liens for Approved Debt or subordinated to the Liens held by Lender on the terms approved by Lender as part of a Permitted Reorganization" — leaving no verb and no discernible condition. Whether Liens securing Approved Debt must actually be subordinated, and on whose terms, cannot be read off the clause as written.

A reorganization qualifies only if it "is consistent in all material respects with the written description provided to Lender by Borrowers prior to the Closing Date" — an extrinsic, unattached and unidentified writing that Section 16.10's integration clause does not incorporate. Whether a particular restructuring was a Permitted Reorganization therefore cannot be determined from the four corners of the instrument.

"Real Property" is defined as real property owned or acquired "by a Borrower or any of its Subsidiaries", yet clauses (b) and (h) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition require each note to be secured by a first-priority Lien on "Real Property" — that is, on property the maker owns, not the Borrower. Applying the defined term where it is used makes the eligibility criteria impossible to satisfy.

Clause (e) sweeps in "any payment ... by Borrower to a holder of Stock in a Borrower or to an Affiliate ... not expressly authorized in this Agreement", which makes the definition circular: whether a payment is a Restricted Payment depends on whether the Agreement authorizes it, and Section 7.10 authorizes it only if it is not a Restricted Payment. Ordinary redemptions of Investor Membership Interests fall in that circle.

The definition states a plain ratio of Obligations to Tangible Net Worth, but Section 7.16(b) tests that ratio "expressed as a percentage" against nine-tenths of one percent, a figure that on any $600,000,000 Tangible Net Worth allows only about $5.4 million of Obligations. Whether the covenant means 0.9 or 90% cannot be settled from the definition alone.

The definition covers "an Approved Title Insurance Company or any settlement agent (including a title company, title agency, attorney or law firm covered by a Closing Protection Letter issued by an Approved Title Insurance Company)", and it is unclear whether the Closing Protection Letter requirement qualifies every settlement agent or only the parenthetical examples. Section 6.18 requires all initial disbursements to go through a Settlement Agent, so the scope matters.

"Solvent" is reduced to a single balance-sheet test — "at fair valuations, the sum of such Person's assets is greater than all of such Person's debts" — with no definition of "debts", no treatment of contingent or unliquidated liabilities, and none of the usual capital-adequacy or ability-to-pay prongs. Section 5.12(a) and clause (q) of the eligibility criteria both turn on the term.

A Subordinated Note is described as "secured by the assets of Fund", but clause (a) of the definition of "Subordinated Debt" admits only "unsecured Indebtedness", and clause (b) admits Approved Debt, which Subordinated Notes evidence. Whether a secured Subordinated Note is Subordinated Debt — and hence added back into Tangible Net Worth — cannot be squared between the two definitions.

The proviso excludes from "Subsidiary" any post-Closing entity not capitalized with a Borrower's assets, any New Fund, and Bar-K, Inc., which leaves the first sentence of Section 7.13 — "Form or acquire any Subsidiary without the prior written consent of Lender" — with almost nothing to operate on. Whether the covenant reaches a newly formed affiliated fund depends entirely on reading the two together.

Clause (b) is triggered when "the aggregate outstanding principal amount of all Notes Receivable of Fund is less than $500,000,000" without saying whether that measures eligible notes, notes net of write-downs, or gross face amount. Because Section 2.1(b) makes the Triggering Event the switch for Lender's reserve rights, how the portfolio is measured is decisive.

The direction that "Borrower" in a financial covenant means "Fund and its Subsidiaries on a consolidated basis" cannot be squared with the definition of "Senior Leverage Ratio", which takes "the outstanding amount of all Obligations of Borrower" — Obligations that Section 2.13 makes the joint and several debt of both Fund and Manager. Whether Manager's borrowings enter the covenant calculation is left to the escape hatch "unless the context clearly requires otherwise".

The last sentence provides that "[a]ny requirement of a writing contained herein or in the other Loan Documents shall be satisfied by the transmission of a Record", which sits against Section 15.1's requirement that amendments and waivers "be in writing and signed by Lender and Administrative Borrower". Whether an electronic Record can effect an amendment or waiver is unresolved between the two.

This section incorporates all schedules by reference, while Section 6.14 provides that no notification "shall ... have the effect of amending or modifying this Agreement or any of the Schedules hereto" — yet Schedules 5.5, 5.8, 5.16, 5.18 and 5.21 are each described in the text as "updated from time to time" and Sections 6.9 and 2.6(c) expressly let the Borrowers amend schedules. Which incorporated version of a schedule governs is not answerable from this section alone.

Lender "agrees to make advances" up to the lesser of the Maximum Revolver Amount and the Borrowing Base, but Sections 2.1(b), 2.1(c) and 2.1(e) and the conditions in Section 3.3 (including the undefined "Material Adverse Change") leave Lender with no enforceable obligation to fund. Whether the commitment in 2.1(a) has content once those provisions are read with it is a whole-instrument question.

The section gives Lender an open right to establish reserves and then promises "not to establish any such reserves unless a Triggering Event has occurred and is continuing", yet Section 10 authorizes Lender, whenever a Borrower fails to pay a third party, to "set up such reserves against the Borrowing Base or the Maximum Revolver Amount as Lender deems necessary" with no Triggering Event condition. The two cannot both be given full effect.

The second limit caps availability plus cash in the Cash Management Accounts at "the aggregate amount of unfunded commitments of Fund to the makers of Notes Receivable", a quantity the agreement never defines, never requires to be reported, and never ties to the Borrowing Base Certificate. How that ceiling is computed, and by whom, is left open.

The notice must be received "no later than noon (Dallas time) on the Business Day that is the requested Funding Date", yet "Business Day" is defined by New York and California bank closings, and the sentence allowing telephonic notice "[a]t Lender's election" leaves it unclear whether the Borrower or the Lender chooses the form of request. Both points bear on whether a given request obliges Lender to fund.

This subsection disapplies the whole Section 2.3(b) waterfall to "any payment made by Borrowers to Lender and specified by Borrowers to be for the payment of specific Obligations then due and payable", which lets the Borrowers reorder the priorities that Section 2.3(b)(i) fixes. Whether a borrower-directed payment overrides the first-to-Lender-Expenses ordering is a conflict between the two subsections.

The conflict rule is confined to "the priority provisions of this Section 2.3" and to conflicts "contained in any other Loan Document", so it resolves nothing about conflicts within this Agreement itself — for example between Section 2.1(b) and Section 10 on reserves. Naming one category of conflict and no other invites an expressio unius reading.

An Overadvance arises whenever Obligations exceed "any of the limitations set forth in Section 2.1", which includes Section 2.1(c)'s cap tied to the Fund's unfunded loan commitments — a figure the agreement never defines or requires to be reported. The Borrowers' duty to repay "immediately" is triggered by a limit whose amount they cannot compute from the instrument.

The default rate is four points above "the per annum rate otherwise applicable to Base Rate Loans" even as to Advances that are LIBOR Rate Loans, and it applies only "at the election of Lender" with no mechanism for making or communicating that election. When and at what rate default interest begins to run is left uncertain.

Interest, fees and Lender Expenses are charged to the Loan Account and "thereafter shall constitute Advances hereunder", but Section 2.1(c) forbids Revolver Usage from exceeding the Maximum Revolver Amount and Section 2.4 makes any excess an immediately repayable Overadvance. Whether Lender's own charges can create a borrower default under those caps is not resolved by either provision.

Clause (ii) requires all Collections to be deposited into a Cash Management Account "in Fund's name", yet Section 2.6(e) and Section 6.17 require escrow monies — including amounts held for Account Debtors — to go into Escrow Accounts, and Section 2.6(e) excepts "accounts belonging to an Account Debtor of Borrower" while Section 6.17 does not. Where funds held for a third party must be deposited cannot be answered from this subsection alone.

Clause (iii) requires each Cash Management Bank to "forward by daily sweep all amounts in the applicable Cash Management Account to the Lender's Account", which cannot be squared with Section 2.6(e)'s permission for Borrower to withdraw escrow funds daily or with Section 2.1(c)(B), which assumes a continuing "aggregate balance of cash in the Cash Management Accounts". A daily total sweep leaves nothing for either provision to operate on.

This subsection makes the Cash Management Accounts "subject to Control Agreements", but Section 2.6(b) requires those same accounts to be governed by "Cash Management Agreements" — a separately defined term with different required provisions. Which agreement must be in place for a Cash Management Account, and whether both are required, is unresolved between the two subsections.

The subsection creates a deposit account defined as the "Escrow Account" and then, in the very next sentences, imposes requirements on "such Cash Management Account" and its deposits, so it is unclear whether an Escrow Account is a Cash Management Account subject to the daily sweep in Section 2.6(b). The Borrower's stated right to withdraw escrow funds daily depends on which label controls.

Lender is authorized to advance "based upon telephonic or other instructions received from anyone purporting to be an Authorized Person", allocating to Borrowers the risk of an impostor without any verification duty or callback procedure. Whether that phrase covers an unauthorized person whom Lender had reason to doubt is left open.

Loan Account statements become "conclusively presumed to be correct" and an account stated unless objected to within 30 days, "absent manifest error" — a term the agreement never defines. What kind of error escapes the conclusive presumption is the whole question in any dispute over the balance owed.

The fee rate is written as "one-half of one percent (0.30%) per annum" — the words and the numeral state two different rates, and elsewhere the agreement equates one-half of one percent with 0.50%. A court would have to decide which controls, and the clause's final cross-reference "(v) $20,000,000" does not match the (i)/(ii)/(A) lettering of the sentence.
